examMarks.basis: Chapter 1 questions in the 2022, 2023 and 2025 papers: 8, 8 and 8 marks

stops.title: Statements and truth values
stops.inShort: A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true (T) or false (F), never both. Questions, exclamations, commands, requests and open sentences (like x + 6 = 9) are not statements.

cards.text: A statement is a declarative (assertive) sentence which is either true or false, but not both simultaneously. Statements are denoted by lowercase letters p, q, r. If a statement is true its truth value is T; if false, its truth value is F.
Interrogative sentences (questions), exclamatory sentences, commands, orders, requests and suggestions cannot be assigned a truth value, so they are not statements in logic.

Sentences whose truth depends on an unspecified variable or opinion — such as 'x + 6 = 9', 'He is tall', or 'Mathematics is an interesting subject' — are open sentences. Because their truth value varies with the situation, open sentences are not statements.

checks.q: Which of the following sentences is a statement in logic?
checks.hint: Eliminate open sentences (unspecified x), commands, and questions.
checks.explain: 'Every equilateral triangle is equiangular' is a declarative sentence that is definitely true (truth value T). The first is an open sentence, the second a command, and the fourth a question.

checks.q: The sentence '5 × 2 = 11' is not a statement in logic because it is mathematically incorrect.
checks.hint: Does a statement have to be true, or simply be definitely true or definitely false?
checks.explain: False. A declarative sentence that is definitely false is still a valid statement in logic — its truth value is simply F.

checks.q: Why is 'x − 3 = 14' NOT a statement in logic?
options: It is an open sentence whose truth value depends on the value of x
Its truth value is always F
checks.hint: Check what happens when x = 17 compared with x = 5.
checks.explain: For x = 17 the equation is true, while for any other x it is false. Since its truth value depends on x, it is an open sentence and not a statement.

stops.title: Connectives: conjunction, disjunction and negation
sections: 1.1.4 Logical Connectives, Simple and Compound Statements
stops.inShort: Conjunction p ∧ q ('and', 'but', 'while') is true only when both p and q are T. Disjunction p ∨ q ('or') is false only when both are F. Negation ~p flips T to F and F to T.

cards.text: Combining two simple statements p and q with 'and' (or 'but', 'while', 'yet') gives the conjunction p ∧ q. It is true if and only if both p and q are true (T ∧ T ≡ T); in the other three cases it is false.
Combining p and q with 'or' gives the disjunction p ∨ q. It is false if and only if both p and q are false (F ∨ F ≡ F); if at least one of p or q is true, p ∨ q is true.
The negation of a statement p, written ~p, is true when p is false and false when p is true. Negating a statement twice returns the original statement: ~(~p) ≡ p.

checks.q: Let p : 'Delhi is in India' and q : 'Dhaka is in Sri Lanka'. Which symbolic form represents 'Delhi is in India, but Dhaka is not in Sri Lanka'?
checks.hint: In logic, the word 'but' acts like 'and' (∧).
checks.explain: 'But' denotes conjunction (∧) and 'not' gives ~q, so the compound statement is p ∧ ~q.

checks.q: The compound statement '4 is odd or 1 is prime' has truth value F.
checks.hint: Check the truth value of each simple statement separately before applying ∨.
checks.explain: True. Both '4 is odd' (F) and '1 is prime' (F — 1 is neither prime nor composite) are false, and F ∨ F ≡ F.

checks.q: If p is T, q is F, and r is F, what is the truth value of (p ∨ q) ∧ ~r?
checks.hint: Substitute T and F into p ∨ q and ~r first, then combine with ∧.
checks.explain: p ∨ q ≡ T ∨ F ≡ T, and ~r ≡ ~F ≡ T. Therefore (p ∨ q) ∧ ~r ≡ T ∧ T ≡ T.

stops.title: Conditional and biconditional statements
stops.inShort: Conditional p → q ('if p then q') is false ONLY when p is T and q is F. Biconditional p ↔ q ('p if and only if q') is true when p and q have the same truth value.

cards.text: The statement 'if p then q', written p → q, has hypothesis (antecedent) p and conclusion (consequent) q. It is false ONLY when p is T and q is F (T → F ≡ F). Whenever p is F, p → q is automatically T.

All of these translate to p → q: 'p implies q', 'p is sufficient for q', 'q is necessary for p', 'q follows from p', and 'p only if q'. Watch out: 'p only if q' means p → q, whereas 'p if q' means q → p.
The statement 'p if and only if q', written p ↔ q, is true when p and q share the same truth value (T ↔ T ≡ T and F ↔ F ≡ T) and false when they differ (T ↔ F ≡ F and F ↔ T ≡ F).

checks.q: What is the truth value of the conditional statement 'If 3 × 5 = 8, then 3 + 5 = 15'?
options: F, because both parts are false
It is not a valid statement
checks.hint: Remember the only row where p → q is false.
checks.explain: Both p ('3 × 5 = 8') and q ('3 + 5 = 15') are false. A conditional p → q is false only when T → F; here F → F ≡ T.

checks.q: The English sentence 'q is necessary for p' is symbolically written as q → p.
checks.hint: Check Balbharati's note on equivalent English phrasings of p → q on page 4.
checks.explain: False. 'q is necessary for p' means p cannot hold without q, so p implies q: p → q. ('p is sufficient for q' also means p → q.)

checks.q: Given p ≡ T, q ≡ T, and r ≡ F, find the truth value of ~(p → q) ↔ (r ∧ q). What is the correct first reduction?
checks.hint: Evaluate the expressions inside each pair of parentheses first: T → T and F ∧ T.
checks.explain: T → T ≡ T and F ∧ T ≡ F, so ~(T → T) ↔ (F ∧ T) reduces to (~T) ↔ F ≡ F ↔ F ≡ T.

stops.title: Statement patterns and truth tables
stops.inShort: A statement pattern combines prime components (p, q, r) with connectives. With n prime components a truth table has 2^{n} rows (4 for 2 letters, 8 for 3 letters). Evaluate in order ~, ∨, ∧, →, ↔.

cards.text: A proper combination of statement letters and logical connectives is called a statement pattern (proposition), and its letters p, q, r are prime components. A truth table with n prime components has 2^{n} rows — 4 rows for 2 letters, 8 rows for 3 letters.

When brackets are omitted, Balbharati lists the connective priority order as ~, ∨, ∧, →, ↔. Negation (~) always binds tightest to the statement immediately following it; parentheses override default priority.

For 2 letters list (T,T), (T,F), (F,T), (F,F). For 3 letters put 4 T's then 4 F's under p; pairs TT, FF, TT, FF under q; and alternating T, F under r. Build columns left-to-right from negations to innermost brackets to the full pattern.

checks.q: How many rows are needed in the truth table of the statement pattern [(~p ∨ q) ∧ (q → r)] → (p → r)?
checks.hint: Count the distinct prime components (p, q, r) and compute 2^{n}.
checks.explain: There are n = 3 prime components (p, q, r), so the truth table has 2³ = 8 rows.

checks.q: For the pattern ~(~p ∧ ~q) ∨ q, what is its truth value in the row where p = F and q = F?
checks.hint: Compute ~p and ~q first, then (~p ∧ ~q), then negate it, then take ∨ q.
checks.explain: When p = F and q = F: ~p = T, ~q = T, so ~p ∧ ~q = T. Negating gives ~(~p ∧ ~q) = F, and F ∨ F = F.

checks.q: To construct the truth table for (~p ∨ q) ↔ ~(p ∧ q), which columns should you compute immediately after p and q?
checks.hint: Look at the smallest sub-expressions inside the two sides of ↔.
checks.explain: The left side needs ~p (to build ~p ∨ q), and the right side needs p ∧ q (to build ~(p ∧ q)).

stops.title: Logical equivalence using truth tables
stops.inShort: Two statement patterns A and B are logically equivalent (A ≡ B) if their final truth-table columns are identical in every row. Always number columns and state which two columns match.

cards.text: Two statement patterns A and B are logically equivalent, written A ≡ B, if they have identical truth values for every possible combination of truth values of their prime components.
Board exams frequently test truth-table proofs of p ∧ q ≡ ~(p → ~q), (p ∧ q) → r ≡ p → (q → r), p → (q ∨ r) ≡ (p → q) ∨ (p → r), and p ↔ q ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q).
Label every column with Roman numerals (I, II, III, …) so that at the end you can write cleanly: 'Columns IV and VI are identical, therefore A ≡ B.' Missing this concluding line can cost half a mark.

checks.q: Which statement pattern is logically equivalent to (p ∧ q) → r?
checks.hint: Check when both patterns are false: only when p = T, q = T, and r = F.
checks.explain: (p ∧ q) → r is false only when p = T, q = T, r = F. The same holds for p → (q → r), so their 8-row columns are identical (Table 1.14, p. 11).

checks.q: If two statement patterns A and B have the same number of T's in their truth-table columns, they must be logically equivalent.
checks.hint: Does the order of T's and F's row by row matter?
checks.explain: False. For A ≡ B, the truth values must match in EVERY corresponding row, not merely have the same count of T's (for instance, p and ~p both have two T's and two F's, yet p ≢ ~p).

checks.q: While proving p ∧ q ≡ ~(p → ~q) by truth table, you have columns for p, q, ~q, p ∧ q, and p → ~q. What is the truth-value column for ~(p → ~q) from row (T,T) down to (F,F)?
checks.hint: p → ~q is F only when p = T and ~q = F (i.e., q = T), so p → ~q is F, T, T, T.
checks.explain: Column p → ~q is F, T, T, T, so its negation ~(p → ~q) is T, F, F, F — identical to p ∧ q.

stops.title: Tautology, contradiction and contingency
stops.inShort: A tautology (t) has all T's in its final truth-table column; a contradiction (c) has all F's; a contingency has a mixture of T and F.

cards.text: A statement pattern whose truth value is T for all possible truth-value combinations of its prime components is a tautology, denoted by t. Classic examples: p ∨ ~p, p → (q → p), and (p → q) ↔ (~p ∨ q).
A statement pattern whose truth value is F for every row of its truth table is a contradiction, denoted by c. Classic examples: p ∧ ~p and (p ∧ q) ∧ (~p ∨ ~q).

A statement pattern that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction — meaning its final column contains at least one T and at least one F — is called a contingency. Example: p ∧ q or [p ∧ (p → ~q)] → q.

checks.q: Classify the statement pattern (p ∧ q) ∧ (~p ∨ ~q).
checks.hint: Notice that ~p ∨ ~q ≡ ~(p ∧ q) by De Morgan's law.
checks.explain: Since ~p ∨ ~q ≡ ~(p ∧ q), the pattern has the form A ∧ ~A, which is F in every row — a contradiction.

checks.q: The statement pattern (p → q) ∨ (q → p) is a tautology.
checks.hint: Can p → q and q → p be false at the same time?
checks.explain: True. p → q is false only at (T, F), where q → p is T; and q → p is false only at (F, T), where p → q is T. So their disjunction is T in all 4 rows.

checks.q: Which of the following statement patterns is a contingency?
checks.hint: Test the row p = T, q = F on each option.
checks.explain: At (T, F), [p ∧ (p → ~q)] → q evaluates to [T ∧ T] → F = F, while at (T, T) it gives F → T = T, so it is a contingency. Options (a) and (b) are tautologies, and (c) is a contradiction.

stops.title: Quantifiers, quantified statements and duals
stops.inShort: Universal quantifier ∀ ('for all') needs every element to satisfy the condition; existential quantifier ∃ ('there exists') needs at least one. To form a dual, swap ∨ ↔ ∧ and t ↔ c while keeping ~ unchanged.

cards.text: The symbol ∀ stands for 'for all' or 'for every'. A statement ∀x ∈ A, P(x) is true only if EVERY element x in set A satisfies P(x). Finding even one counterexample in A makes the statement false.

The symbol ∃ stands for 'there exists at least one' or 'for some'. A statement ∃x ∈ A such that P(x) is true as soon as AT LEAST ONE element x in A satisfies P(x); it is false only if NO element in A does.
For patterns containing ∨, ∧, t and c, the dual is obtained by interchanging ∨ with ∧, ∧ with ∨, t with c, and c with t. Never change ~ or the statement letters p, q, r when writing a dual.

checks.q: What is the dual of the statement pattern c ∨ [p ∧ (q ∨ ~r)]?
checks.hint: Swap c ↔ t and ∨ ↔ ∧, but leave ~r completely untouched.
checks.explain: Replacing c → t, ∨ → ∧, and ∧ → ∨ while keeping p, q, ~r unchanged yields t ∧ [p ∨ (q ∧ ~r)].

checks.q: If A = {3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12}, then the quantified statement '∀x ∈ A, x² + x is an even number' has truth value T.
checks.hint: Factor x² + x as x(x + 1) — the product of two consecutive integers.
checks.explain: True. For every integer x, x(x + 1) is the product of two consecutive integers, one of which is always even; hence x² + x is even for every x ∈ A.

checks.q: If A = {3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12}, which quantified statement is FALSE?
checks.hint: Can the square of any real number in A ever be negative?
checks.explain: For every real number x, x² ≥ 0, so no element of A satisfies x² < 0. The other three are true (x = 9 for (a), x = 11 or 12 for (b), and min 2(3) + 9 = 15 > 14 for (c)).

stops.title: Negations of compound and quantified statements
stops.inShort: De Morgan's laws: ~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q and ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q. Negation of conditional: ~(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ~q. Negation of biconditional: ~(p ↔ q) ≡ (p ∧ ~q) ∨ (q ∧ ~p). Quantifiers flip ∀ ↔ ∃.

cards.text: The negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of negations: ~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q. The negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of negations: ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q.
The negation of p → q is NOT an implication: ~(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ~q ('p and not q'). The negation of p ↔ q is ~(p ↔ q) ≡ (p ∧ ~q) ∨ (q ∧ ~p).
To negate a quantified statement, replace ∀ ('all' / 'for every') by ∃ ('some' / 'there exists') and vice versa, and negate the condition. Remember: negation of > is ≤, of < is ≥, of = is ≠.

checks.q: What is the negation of 'If it is raining, then we will go and play football'?
options: If it is not raining, then we will not go or not play football.
It is raining and we will not go or not play football.
It is not raining and we will go and play football.
It is raining or we will not go and not play football.
checks.hint: Write the statement as p → (q ∧ r), then use ~(A → B) ≡ A ∧ ~B and De Morgan's law.
checks.explain: ~[p → (q ∧ r)] ≡ p ∧ ~(q ∧ r) ≡ p ∧ (~q ∨ ~r): 'It is raining and we will not go or not play football.'

checks.q: The negation of 'The number is neither odd nor a perfect square' is 'The number is odd or a perfect square'.
checks.hint: 'Neither p nor q' is symbolically ~p ∧ ~q.
checks.explain: True. 'Neither p nor q' is ~p ∧ ~q. Its negation by De Morgan's law is ~(~p ∧ ~q) ≡ p ∨ q.

checks.q: Find the negation of '∀x ∈ N, 2x + 1 is odd'. Which step produces the correct negation?
options: Replace ∀ with ∃ and negate the predicate: ∃x ∈ N such that 2x + 1 is not odd
Keep ∀ and negate the predicate: ∀x ∈ N, 2x + 1 is not odd
Replace ∀ with ∃ and keep the predicate: ∃x ∈ N such that 2x + 1 is odd
checks.hint: Negating a universal statement flips ∀ to ∃ and negates the condition.
checks.explain: Negating '∀x ∈ N, P(x)' always gives '∃x ∈ N such that ~P(x)': '∃x ∈ N such that 2x + 1 is not odd.'

stops.title: Converse, inverse and contrapositive
stops.inShort: From p → q: Converse is q → p, Inverse is ~p → ~q, Contrapositive is ~q → ~p. Note that p → q ≡ ~q → ~p (contrapositive), and q → p ≡ ~p → ~q (converse ≡ inverse).

cards.text: Given a conditional p → q: its converse swaps the two parts (q → p); its inverse negates both parts (~p → ~q); and its contrapositive swaps AND negates both parts (~q → ~p).
Truth tables show two vital equivalences: every implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive (p → q ≡ ~q → ~p), and the converse is logically equivalent to the inverse (q → p ≡ ~p → ~q).

In 'A family becomes literate if the woman in it is literate', the condition after 'if' is p ('the woman is literate') and the result is q ('the family becomes literate'). Always rewrite as 'If p then q' before forming converse, inverse, or contrapositive.

checks.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If a function is differentiable, then it is continuous'?
options: If a function is continuous, then it is differentiable.
If a function is not differentiable, then it is not continuous.
If a function is not continuous, then it is not differentiable.
A function is differentiable and not continuous.
checks.hint: Contrapositive of p → q is ~q → ~p (swap and negate both).
checks.explain: With p : differentiable and q : continuous, ~q → ~p reads 'If a function is not continuous, then it is not differentiable.'

checks.q: For any statements p and q, the converse (q → p) and the inverse (~p → ~q) are logically equivalent.
checks.hint: Think of the inverse ~p → ~q as the contrapositive of q → p.
checks.explain: True. Since any conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, q → p ≡ ~p → ~q.

checks.q: Find the inverse of the statement pattern (p ∨ q) → (p ∧ q). Which simplified form is correct?
checks.hint: The inverse of A → B is ~A → ~B; then apply De Morgan's laws to both sides.
checks.explain: Inverse is ~(p ∨ q) → ~(p ∧ q). Applying De Morgan's laws gives (~p ∧ ~q) → (~p ∨ ~q).

stops.title: Algebra of statements — proofs without truth tables
stops.inShort: Use the 10 named laws of algebra of statements (Idempotent, Commutative, Associative, Distributive, De Morgan's, Identity, Complement, Absorption, Conditional, Biconditional) to simplify or prove equivalences without truth tables.

cards.text: Distributive laws let you factor out or expand across ∧ and ∨: p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) and p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r). Absorption collapses p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p and p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p. Idempotent gives p ∧ p ≡ p and p ∨ p ≡ p.
Complement laws produce constants: p ∨ ~p ≡ t and p ∧ ~p ≡ c. Identity laws then remove constants: p ∧ t ≡ p, p ∨ c ≡ p, p ∧ c ≡ c, and p ∨ t ≡ t.

Before applying algebra laws, replace arrows using the Conditional law (p → q ≡ ~p ∨ q) and Biconditional law (p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p) ≡ (~p ∨ q) ∧ (~q ∨ p)). The Conditional law also rewrites 'If p then q' without 'if...then' as '~p or q'.

checks.q: Rewrite 'If prices increase, then wages rise' without using 'if ... then'.
options: Prices do not increase or wages rise.
Prices increase and wages do not rise.
Prices do not increase and wages rise.
checks.hint: Use the Conditional law: p → q ≡ ~p ∨ q.
checks.explain: Let p : prices increase, q : wages rise. By the Conditional law p → q ≡ ~p ∨ q: 'Prices do not increase or wages rise.'

checks.q: To simplify (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ~q) without a truth table, what is the best first step?
options: Factor out p using the Distributive law: p ∨ (q ∧ ~q)
Apply De Morgan's law to both brackets
Use the Idempotent law to drop q
checks.hint: Notice both brackets begin with 'p ∨ ...'.
checks.explain: By the Distributive law, (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ~q) ≡ p ∨ (q ∧ ~q) ≡ p ∨ c [Complement law] ≡ p [Identity law].

checks.q: By the Identity law, p ∨ t ≡ p and p ∧ c ≡ p.
checks.hint: Test p = F in p ∨ t and p = T in p ∧ c.
checks.explain: False. The Identity law states p ∨ t ≡ t and p ∧ c ≡ c (whereas p ∧ t ≡ p and p ∨ c ≡ p).

stops.title: Switching circuits, switching tables and Misc Exercise 1
sections: 1.5 Application of Logic to Switching Circuits
stops.inShort: Switch S_{1} corresponds to p and complementary switch S'_{1} to ~p. Series switches mean ∧, parallel switches mean ∨. In switching tables 1 = closed/ON and 0 = open/OFF; all 1s (t) means lamp always glows, all 0s (c) means it never glows.

cards.text: Each switch S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3} is represented by a statement letter p, q, r ('switch is closed/ON'). Complementary switches S'_{1}, S'_{2} always have the opposite state and correspond to ~p, ~q. In an input-output (switching) table, 1 means ON/glows and 0 means OFF/does not glow.

Two switches S_{1} and S_{2} connected in series allow current only when both are closed, so they represent conjunction p ∧ q. Two switches in parallel allow current if at least one is closed, so they represent disjunction p ∨ q.

To minimise the number of switches, write the symbolic form and simplify it using Algebra of Statements, then draw the simpler circuit. If the final switching-table column is all 1s (≡ t), the lamp always glows; if all 0s (≡ c), the lamp never glows regardless of switch positions.

checks.q: In a switching circuit, a parallel combination of S_{1} and S_{2} is connected in series with S'_{1}. What is its symbolic logical form?
checks.hint: Parallel translates to ∨, series translates to ∧, and S'_{1} is ~p.
checks.explain: S_{1} and S_{2} in parallel give (p ∨ q). Connecting this block in series with S'_{1} (~p) gives (p ∨ q) ∧ ~p.

checks.q: A switching circuit has symbolic form [p ∨ (~q ∨ ~r)] ∧ [p ∨ (q ∧ r)] using 6 switches. After simplifying it using Algebra of Statements, how many switches are needed in the equivalent minimal circuit?
checks.hint: Use the Distributive law to factor out 'p ∨', then apply De Morgan's law to (~q ∨ ~r).
checks.explain: [p ∨ (~q ∨ ~r)] ∧ [p ∨ (q ∧ r)] ≡ p ∨ [(~q ∨ ~r) ∧ (q ∧ r)] ≡ p ∨ [~(q ∧ r) ∧ (q ∧ r)] ≡ p ∨ c ≡ p, which requires only 1 switch (S_{1}).

checks.q: If the final column of a switching table consists entirely of 1s, the lamp will always glow irrespective of the status of the switches.
checks.hint: Recall that 1 represents current flowing (lamp ON) and all 1s corresponds to a tautology t.
checks.explain: True. Every combination of switch states outputs 1, meaning the circuit is always closed and the lamp always glows.

board.text: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} then which of the following is not true?
board.answer: (c) ∀x ∈ A, x + 6 ≥ 9. Check each option: (a) true for x = 5 since 5 + 3 = 8; (b) true for x = 1 since 1 + 2 = 3 < 9; (c) false for x = 1 since 1 + 6 = 7 < 9 (and for x = 2, 2 + 6 = 8 < 9); (d) true for x = 1 since 1 + 6 = 7 < 10. Therefore (c) is not true.

points.text: Identify counterexample x = 1 ∈ A giving x + 6 = 7 < 9, so ∀x ∈ A, x + 6 ≥ 9 is false
Write the correct option with letter: (c) ∀x ∈ A, x + 6 ≥ 9

board.text: Write the negation of the statement : '∃n ∈ N such that n + 8 > 11'

points.text: Replace ∃ with ∀ and negate > to ≤: ∀n ∈ N, n + 8 ≤ 11

board.text: Using truth table, prove that the statement patterns p ↔ q and (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q) are logically equivalent.
board.answer: Prepare the 4-row truth table with columns I: p, II: q, III: ~p, IV: ~q, V: p ↔ q, VI: p ∧ q, VII: ~p ∧ ~q, VIII: (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q). Row (T,T): V = T, VI = T, VII = F, VIII = T. Row (T,F): V = F, VI = F, VII = F, VIII = F. Row (F,T): V = F, VI = F, VII = F, VIII = F. Row (F,F): V = T, VI = F, VII = T, VIII = T. Since columns V and VIII are identical (T, F, F, T), p ↔ q ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q).

points.text: Complete 4-row truth table with accurate columns for p ↔ q, p ∧ q, ~p ∧ ~q, and (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q)
Note that the columns for p ↔ q and (p ∧ q) ∨ (~p ∧ ~q) are identical (T, F, F, T) and conclude logical equivalence

board.text: Express the following switching circuit in the symbolic form of logic. Construct the switching table and interpret it : [Circuit: A parallel combination of switch S_{1} (upper branch) and switch S_{2} (lower branch) is connected in series with switch S'_{1} and switch S'_{2}, all wired in a closed loop with a battery and lamp L.]
board.answer: Let p : switch S_{1} is closed, q : switch S_{2} is closed, ~p : switch S'_{1} is closed, ~q : switch S'_{2} is closed. Symbolic form: (p ∨ q) ∧ ~p ∧ ~q. Switching table for (p, q): (1,1) → p ∨ q = 1, ~p = 0, ~q = 0, output = 0; (1,0) → p ∨ q = 1, ~p = 0, ~q = 1, output = 0; (0,1) → p ∨ q = 1, ~p = 1, ~q = 0, output = 0; (0,0) → p ∨ q = 0, ~p = 1, ~q = 1, output = 0. Interpretation: Since all entries in the last column are 0, the lamp will never glow irrespective of the status of the switches.

points.text: Define statement letters p, q and write the symbolic form (p ∨ q) ∧ ~p ∧ ~q
Construct the complete 4-row switching table (1/0 entries) obtaining 0 in every row of the final column
Interpretation: the lamp will not glow irrespective of the status of the switches

board.text: If p ∧ q is F, p → q is F then the truth values of p and q are ______ respectively.
board.answer: (b) T, F. The implication p → q is false only when p is T and q is F; with p = T and q = F, p ∧ q = T ∧ F = F, satisfying both conditions.

points.text: Use conditional truth table: p → q is F only when p ≡ T and q ≡ F (which also makes p ∧ q ≡ F)
Write the correct option with letter: (b) T, F

board.text: Write inverse and contrapositive of the following statement : If x < y then x² < y²
